e.t: This Hebrew noun means “corn,” referring to the food crop or its harvested produce. It appears nine times in the Old Testament corpus, especially in Genesis, where it is associated with obtaining and handling this staple food. The word also occurs in Nehemiah and Amos, showing that its ordinary sense remains connected with food supplies and trade rather than an abstract idea.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “bough.” It names a physical part of a tree rather than an action, quality, or person. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Judges 9:48–49. Its use is concrete and ordinary, referring to something associated with trees and treated as a physical object in the passage. The word does not itself express an abstract idea or spiritual condition.

This Hebrew word means “youth,” referring to the period of being young. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Ecclesiastes 11:10. As a word naming youth, it points to a person’s early years rather than to a specific action or object. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the period of youth.

This Hebrew word means “on.” It functions as a short relational word, connecting a surrounding phrase with what it relates to rather than naming an object, person, or action by itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times in three different verses. Its precise contribution in any one sentence depends on the words around it, but its basic sense is the relational term “on.”

It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Leviticus 19:19 and Deuteronomy 22:11. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic role is to show a relationship between connected terms.

The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 40:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, but its basic meaning is “navel.”

This word occurs 51 times in the Hebrew Old Testament.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “beacon,” an upright structure that can serve as a visible marker. It occurs three times in the Old Testament, in Isaiah and Ezekiel. Its use includes both an object associated with visibility and a structure connected with a ship, so the surrounding sentence determines its precise function. The central idea remains something raised upright and identifiable from a distance.

This Hebrew word refers to a place or location. It identifies a particular spot or designated area, especially in passages concerning the temple and the movement or setting of kingdoms. It occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra and Daniel. Its use in Ezra includes references to the temple’s place, while Daniel uses it in descriptions involving kingdoms and their position. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Betah is a Hebrew proper name identifying a place. It is not presented here as a general action, quality, or object-word, but as the name of a specific location. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 8:8. Because the available material does not include the verse text or a definition beyond the name itself, its precise geographical identity cannot be established from this word alone. Its role is therefore best understood as a place designation named Betah.
